record.paper_title: Trimer Covers in the Triangular Grid: Twenty Mostly Open Problems
record.original_question: For tilings of a finite simply-connected region in the hexagonal grid by stones and bones, there are two natural local 2-flip moves: one replaces two oppositely oriented stones by two bones, and the other replaces a stone-and-bone pair by a stone of the same orientation together with a bone of a different orientation. Can every such tiling be transformed into every other such tiling by a finite succession of these 2-flips?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider the hexagonal grid (the regular tiling of the plane by unit hexagons). A "stone" is a tile consisting of three pairwise-adjacent hexagonal cells meeting at a common vertex; there are two orientations of stones (the "left" stone and the "right" stone, related by 180° rotation). A "bone" is a tile consisting of three hexagonal cells arranged in a straight line; there are three orientations of bones (horizontal, rising at 60°, and falling at -60°). Together stones and bones constitute the five "stones-and-bones" prototiles, each covering three cells of the hexagonal grid.

Let R be a finite simply-connected region of the hexagonal grid, and consider tilings of R by congruent copies of the five prototiles above. Define two local "2-flip" moves on such tilings:

(F1) Replace two stones of opposite orientations (one left and one right) that together occupy six cells forming a region tilable by two bones, by two bones covering the same six cells; or perform the reverse replacement.

(F2) Replace a pair consisting of one stone and one bone, occupying six cells, by another pair consisting of a stone of the same orientation and a bone of a different orientation covering the same six cells.

Two tilings of R are said to be "2-flip equivalent" if one can be obtained from the other by a finite sequence of moves of types (F1) and (F2). Question: For every finite simply-connected region R of the hexagonal grid, is it the case that any two tilings of R by stones and bones are 2-flip equivalent?
artifact.status_search_result: The general question appears to remain open. A restricted case — when one of the three bone orientations is forbidden (type 112) — is known to follow from Sheffield's connectivity theorem for ribbon tilings. Recent work (2025) on tilability of the hexagonal grid by stones, bones, and snakes via dimer models extends related results but does not resolve the full 2-flip connectivity question.

status_evidence.title: Stones, Bones, and Snakes: Tilability of the hexagonal grid via the double dimer model
status_evidence.snippet: Introduces tilings by bones, stones, and snakes and gives necessary conditions on tilability via single and double dimer models.
status_evidence.claim: Recent related work addresses tilability conditions but not the full 2-flip connectivity problem.

status_evidence.title: Stones, Bones, and Snakes (HTML)
status_evidence.snippet: If one restricts to tilings of type 112 (prohibiting one of the three orientations of bones), then the claim is true; Sheffield proved an equivalent claim in the context of ribbon tilings.
status_evidence.claim: The 2-flip connectivity is known in the restricted setting where one bone orientation is forbidden, by Sheffield's ribbon-tiling theorem; the general case is stated as open.
